what: Methanex is the world’s largest producer and supplier of methanol, a basic chemical made mostly from natural gas. Its plants are in New Zealand, Trinidad, Chile, Egypt, Canada and the US Gulf Coast, and it runs its own fleet of ships to deliver methanol to customers worldwide.
customers: Chemical producers that turn methanol into formaldehyde, acetic acid and plastics, Chinese plants that convert methanol into olefins, fuel blenders and increasingly shipping lines using methanol as a marine fuel.
money: Produced methanol plus volumes bought from other producers and resold through its distribution network.
moat: Global scale, low-cost gas contracts at several plants and a distribution and shipping network that lets it serve customers reliably from multiple regions.
risks: Methanol prices are set largely by marginal demand from Chinese methanol-to-olefins plants and swing with the economy.
Natural gas supply disruptions in Trinidad, New Zealand and Egypt have repeatedly cut output.
More debt after the acquisition of OCI’s methanol business leaves less room in a downturn.
opportunities: Methanol as a low-carbon marine fuel could add a new source of demand over the next decade.
The acquired US and European plants add gas-advantaged capacity and diversify supply away from troubled regions.
watch: The methanol price against the gas cost at each plant. Methanex’s earnings are almost entirely that spread multiplied by the tonnes it can produce.
view: The screen shows Methanex at about 3.4 times free cash flow and 13 times earnings, and the first number should not be trusted. Free cash flow of $1.4 billion on $4.7 billion of revenue is not a run rate for a methanol producer; it reflects timing, working capital and the consolidation of the newly acquired OCI plants. A more honest frame is EV/EBITDA of about 4.8 times, which is cheap for a business at an average point in the cycle but not obviously so at a good one.

Methanex is a pure commodity producer, and the investment turns on two things: the methanol price, set largely by what Chinese olefins plants will pay, and gas supply at its plants, which has been the company’s chronic problem. Trinidad and New Zealand have both suffered gas curtailments, and Egypt’s gas exports are unreliable. The OCI acquisition matters mainly because it adds plants in places with dependable gas, which should reduce the number of years in which Methanex has the market but cannot make the product.

With analysts’ targets about 28% above the price, the market is sceptical of the acquisition and of the cycle. I think the scepticism is reasonable but slightly overdone: the company has a long record of buying back shares cheaply in downturns and paying out in good years. This is a cyclical worth owning near the bottom of the methanol price range, and the low multiple is only cheap if you believe gas supply at the older plants holds up.
bull: Methanol prices recover with Chinese demand, the acquired plants run reliably, and strong cash flow pays down acquisition debt quickly.
bear: Gas curtailments return at Trinidad and New Zealand while methanol prices stay weak, and the extra debt turns a normal down-cycle into a strained one.
